nkp.welcome.intro:
Welcome to the NKP Fundamentals lab.
You will carve out your own slice of a shared Nutanix Kubernetes Platform, give a real application persistent storage, and then hand the deployment over to GitOps.
No prior Kubernetes needed. We go one small step at a time, and you press Enter to move on when you are ready.
<input/>
nkp.welcome.prompt:
Your instructor assigned you a user number (user01, user02, ...).
Enter just the number: <input var='UserNum'/>
nkp.tour.intro:
Before touching anything real, take the guided tour of the NKP console.
It is a sandbox, so nothing you click there reaches the cluster.
<input/>
nkp.tour.demo:
Open the quick tour from the bootcamp page and look around: the Global scope at the top, workspaces below it, and projects inside those.
Close the sandbox when you reach the end, then come back here.
nkp.access.console: You are user{UserNum}. Sign in to the NKP console as this user. {DashboardUrl} Accept the self-signed certificate, choose Log in with ntnxlab.local, and use your credentials. Do not add the domain to your username.
nkp.mt.intro:
Now a little platform thinking.
One cluster is shared by many teams, so NKP keeps them apart in two ways.
<white>Workspaces</white> group whole clusters, which is how you separate customers.
<white>Projects</white> hand out namespaces inside those clusters, which is how you separate teams.
<input/>
nkp.mt.diagram:
Here is how the scopes nest:
<image src='multitenancy_diagram.2923c533.png' alt='NKP scopes: Global, Workspaces, and Projects.'/>
nkp.ws.intro:
Start at the level above projects: the <white>Workspace</white>.
It groups clusters and shows their health, cost, and projects in one place.
<input/>
nkp.ws.explore:
Open Global, then Workspaces, then <white>Default Workspace</white>, and have a look around.
You will find the clusters staged for the rest of this lab.
<image src='workspace_dashboard.a5f37201.png' alt='The Default Workspace dashboard.'/>
nkp.project.intro:
Time to claim your own space.
Creating a <white>Project</white> gives you a namespace named <white>user{UserNum}</white>, federated out to the workload cluster.
<input/>
nkp.project.form:
In the Default Workspace, choose <white>Projects</white>, then <white>Create Project</white>:
  Project Name:  <white>user{UserNum}</white>
  ID / Namespace:  <white>user{UserNum}</white>  (the same)
  Clusters:  <white>Manually Selected Clusters</white>
  Selected Cluster:  <white>workload01</white>  (only)
Then Continue to Project.
<image src='project_create_02.39ccb846.png' alt='The Create Project form with name, namespace, and cluster selection.'/>
<input/>
nkp.project.prompt: When your project exists, type Ok to verify: <input var='Ok'/>
nkp.storage.intro:
Time for real storage.
Apps that keep data need <white>persistent storage</white>, and a pod can be rescheduled onto another node at any moment, so that storage cannot live on the node.
NKP ships the Nutanix CSI driver, so Kubernetes asks Nutanix for volumes on demand.
<input/>
nkp.storage.diagram:
You will build the classic pair: MySQL on <white>block</white> storage, and a WordPress frontend on <white>shared file</white> storage.
<image src='wordpress_diagram.59a9a0b6.png' alt='WordPress frontend with a MySQL backend on persistent storage.'/>
nkp.sc.intro:
Open the <white>Kubernetes Dashboard</white> for workload01.
In your project: Clusters, the workload01 menu, then Kubernetes. Re-authenticate and accept the certificate.
<image src='open_k8s_dashboard.efdcbc6c.png' alt='Opening the Kubernetes dashboard from the project clusters page.'/>
<input/>
nkp.sc.namespace:
At the top, change the namespace to <white>user{UserNum}</white>.
There are no resources yet. This clean, private space is yours.
<image src='k8s_dashboard_ns.03dd6ac1.gif' alt='Selecting your user namespace in the Kubernetes Dashboard.'/>
<input/>
nkp.sc.classes:
Under Config and Storage, open Storage Classes.
<white>nutanix-volume</white> is the default: block storage, one writer at a time. Any request that does not name a class lands here.
<white>nutanix-files</white> is staged too, and you will need it shortly.
<image src='k8s_dashboard_sc.3bb5f540.png' alt='The StorageClasses list showing nutanix-volume as default.'/>
nkp.block.intro:
Your first stateful workload.
You will deploy MySQL. It asks for a 20Gi volume through a <white>PersistentVolumeClaim</white>.
Since no StorageClass is named, the default <white>nutanix-volume</white> catches the request and Nutanix provisions a real volume group.
<input/>
nkp.block.manifest: With namespace user{UserNum} selected, click the + in the dashboard, paste this manifest, and Upload: apiVersion: v1 kind: Secret metadata: name: mysql-pass type: Opaque stringData: password: nutanix/4u --- apiVersion: v1 kind: Service metadata: name: wordpress-mysql labels: app: wordpress spec: ports: - port: 3306 selector: app: wordpress tier: mysql clusterIP: None --- apiVersion: v1 kind: PersistentVolumeClaim metadata: name: mysql-pv-claim labels: app: wordpress spec: accessModes: - ReadWriteOnce resources: requests: storage: 20Gi --- apiVersion: apps/v1 kind: Deployment metadata: name: wordpress-mysql labels: app: wordpress spec: selector: matchLabels: app: wordpress tier: mysql strategy: type: Recreate template: metadata: labels: app: wordpress tier: mysql spec: containers: - image: mysql:8.0 name: mysql env: - name: MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD valueFrom: secretKeyRef: name: mysql-pass key: password - name: MYSQL_DATABASE value: wordpress - name: MYSQL_USER value: wordpress - name: MYSQL_PASSWORD valueFrom: secretKeyRef: name: mysql-pass key: password ports: - containerPort: 3306 name: mysql volumeMounts: - name: mysql-persistent-storage mountPath: /var/lib/mysql volumes: - name: mysql-persistent-storage persistentVolumeClaim: claimName: mysql-pv-claim
nkp.block.apply:
Wait for the workloads to go green. The PVC <white>mysql-pv-claim</white> should become <white>Bound</white>.
<image src='k8s_dashboard_mysql_status.2470fe92.png' alt='The MySQL workloads showing green, healthy status.'/>
<image src='k8s_dashboard_mysql_pvc.9b901e30.gif' alt='The persistent volume claim created for MySQL.'/>
<input/>
nkp.block.prompt: When your MySQL is running and the PVC is Bound, type Ok to verify: <input var='Ok'/>
nkp.file.intro:
MySQL has its volume, but the WordPress frontend is a different problem.
It runs <white>two replicas</white>, and both need the same files: uploads, plugins, themes.
Block storage cannot do that, only one node may write to it. You need <white>ReadWriteMany</white>, which is what Nutanix Files provides.
<input/>
nkp.file.manifest: Same dashboard, same namespace. Paste and Upload. Notice this claim names nutanix-files explicitly, unlike the MySQL one: apiVersion: v1 kind: Service metadata: name: wordpress labels: app: wordpress spec: ports: - port: 80 selector: app: wordpress tier: frontend clusterIP: None --- apiVersion: v1 kind: PersistentVolumeClaim metadata: name: wp-pv-claim labels: app: wordpress spec: storageClassName: nutanix-files accessModes: - ReadWriteMany resources: requests: storage: 20Gi --- apiVersion: apps/v1 kind: Deployment metadata: name: wordpress labels: app: wordpress spec: replicas: 2 selector: matchLabels: app: wordpress tier: frontend strategy: type: Recreate template: metadata: labels: app: wordpress tier: frontend spec: containers: - image: wordpress:apache name: wordpress env: - name: WORDPRESS_DB_HOST value: wordpress-mysql - name: WORDPRESS_DB_PASSWORD valueFrom: secretKeyRef: name: mysql-pass key: password - name: WORDPRESS_DB_USER value: wordpress ports: - containerPort: 80 name: wordpress volumeMounts: - name: wordpress-persistent-storage mountPath: /var/www/html volumes: - name: wordpress-persistent-storage persistentVolumeClaim: claimName: wp-pv-claim
nkp.file.apply:
Wait for both wordpress pods to go green.
On the Nutanix side this claim became an NFS share on Nutanix Files, which is exactly why two pods can mount it at once.
<image src='k8s_dashboard_wordpress.1a4327b3.png' alt='Pasting the WordPress manifest into the dashboard and uploading it.'/>
<image src='files_shares.46da30f8.png' alt='The matching share visible in Nutanix Files.'/>
<input/>
nkp.file.prompt: When both wordpress replicas are running, type Ok to verify: <input var='Ok'/>
nkp.wping.intro:
WordPress is running, but only from inside the cluster.
An <white>Ingress</white> gives it a hostname on the outside, routed by the <white>kommander-traefik</white> controller.
<input/>
nkp.wping.manifest: Apply this, replacing <ingress-lb-ip> with the workload01 ingress IP from your connection page (it ends in .19). The host must carry your own number, or you will collide with your neighbour: apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1 kind: Ingress metadata: name: wordpress spec: ingressClassName: kommander-traefik rules: - host: wordpress{UserNum}.<ingress-lb-ip>.sslip.io http: paths: - path: / pathType: Prefix backend: service: name: wordpress port: number: 80 Then open the URL from the Hosts column and accept the certificate. Do not run the WordPress installer.
nkp.wping.prompt: When your WordPress page answers on its hostname, type Ok to verify: <input var='Ok'/>
nkp.recap.fundamentals:
That is the foundation.
You took a slice of a shared cluster with a Project, ran a stateful app on Nutanix Volumes, gave its scale-out tier a shared Nutanix Files volume, and published it through Traefik.
Next: watching it.
nkp.metrics.intro:
An app you cannot see is an app you cannot run in production.
NKP ships <white>Grafana</white> with 27 dashboards already wired up, nothing to set up on your side.
<input/>
nkp.metrics.explore:
Open your project, then the Grafana dashboard for workload01.
Start on the cluster overview, then find the workload dashboard and filter the namespace down to <white>user{UserNum}</white>. Your WordPress and MySQL pods are in there.
<image src='metrics_2.627c6a95.png' alt='Opening Grafana from the project.'/>
<image src='metrics_3.5e5e8090.gif' alt='Filtering the workload dashboard down to your namespace.'/>
nkp.insights.intro:
Dashboards tell you what happened. <white>NKP Insights</white> tells you what it means.
It watches events and metrics across the fleet and raises anomalies with a root cause, a fix, and the practice that avoids it next time.
<input/>
nkp.insights.explore:
Open Insights for the Default Workspace, filter to <white>Configuration</white> issues, and open a CPU throttling anomaly (or anything that catches your eye).
Read the root cause and the recommendation, not just the alert.
<image src='insights_4.95c8633c.png' alt='A CPU throttling anomaly in NKP Insights.'/>
<image src='Insights_7.0bcfac6e.gif' alt='Following an insight through to the underlying dashboards.'/>
nkp.cost.intro:
The last question production always asks: what does this cost?
<white>OpenCost</white> breaks cluster spend down by namespace, deployment, and label, which is what makes showback possible.
<input/>
nkp.cost.explore:
Open the OpenCost dashboard from your project and look at the last 7 days.
Then narrow it to your own namespace and see what your WordPress stack actually costs.
<image src='kubecost_overview.66733a48.png' alt='The OpenCost overview for the last seven days.'/>
<image src='kubecost_savings.8defcaa7.png' alt='Cost broken down by node, namespace, and container.'/>
nkp.recap.observability:
Metrics, anomalies, and cost, all scoped to the project you created.
Now the part that changes how you deploy.
nkp.gitops.intro:
Everything so far you did by hand: pasting manifests, clicking through forms.
That does not survive contact with a real environment. Nobody can say what changed, or why, or put it back.
<white>GitOps</white> inverts it: the repository is the truth, and <white>Flux</white> makes the cluster match it.
<input/>
nkp.gitops.source:
In your project, open the <white>Continuous Deployment (CD)</white> tab and click <white>Add GitOps Source</white>:
  ID (name):  <white>online-boutique</white>
  Repository URL:  <white>https://github.com/nutanixdev/nkp-microservices-demo.git</white>
  Git Ref Type:  <white>Branch</white>
  Branch Name:  <white>main</white>
  Path:  <white>./release/without-istio</white>
The path must be exact. Save.
<image src='add_source.9521f23c.png' alt='The Add GitOps Source button on the project CD tab.'/>
<image src='boutique_gitops_source.609165ea.gif' alt='Filling in the GitOps source configuration.'/>
<input/>
nkp.gitops.prompt: When the source is saved and syncing, type Ok to verify: <input var='Ok'/>
nkp.boutique.intro:
You did not deploy anything. Flux did, from that repository.
What is arriving is an online boutique: <white>11 microservices</white> in different languages, plus a redis for the shopping cart.
<input/>
nkp.boutique.explore:
Open the Kubernetes dashboard for workload01, switch to namespace <white>user{UserNum}</white>, and watch the Workloads section fill up.
When the pods are green, go to Services and open the URL on <white>frontend-external</white>.
<image src='boutique_app.ca253528.gif' alt='The boutique workloads appearing in the namespace.'/>
<image src='frontend_boutique.ce7f8937.png' alt='The online boutique storefront.'/>
<input/>
nkp.boutique.prompt: When the boutique is up and serving, type Ok to verify: <input var='Ok'/>
nkp.dyn.intro:
One cluster is a demo. A fleet is the job.
Right now your project names workload01 explicitly. Add a fiftieth cluster and someone has to remember to edit fifty projects.
Instead, describe the clusters you want by <white>label</white> and let NKP keep up.
<input/>
nkp.dyn.edit:
Edit your project and switch cluster assignment from manual to <white>Dynamic</white>, then add the label:
  Key:  <white>infraId</white>   (capital I)
  Value:  <white>pc</white>
<white>workload02</white> already carries that label, so it joins the moment you save. The boutique follows on its own.
<image src='dynamic_select.82f4d127.gif' alt='Switching the project to dynamic cluster assignment.'/>
<image src='two_cluster.db371afc.png' alt='Both workload clusters now assigned to the project.'/>
<input/>
nkp.dyn.prompt: When workload02 has joined and the boutique is running there too, type Ok to verify: <input var='Ok'/>
nkp.conclusion.takeaways:
That is the bootcamp.
You carved a tenant out of a shared platform, ran a stateful application on Nutanix storage, published it, watched it, priced it, and then handed deployment to Git and watched it spread across a fleet on its own.
The optional labs that follow are yours to take or skip.
nkp.ndk.intro:
Optional: business continuity.
<white>Nutanix Data Services for Kubernetes</white> adds application-aware snapshots and replication, so a stateful app is recovered as a unit rather than volume by volume.
<input/>
nkp.ndk.demo:
Take the NDK sandbox lab from the bootcamp page, then close it and come back.
Nothing there touches your cluster.
nkp.ide.intro:
Optional track: the same ideas from a terminal instead of the console.
Your environment includes an admin VM running a web IDE, which is where <white>kubectl</white> lives.
<input/>
nkp.ide.terminal:
Open the admin VM address over HTTPS (it is on your connection page), accept the certificate, then open a terminal: the menu icon, Terminal, New Terminal.
<image src='ide-url.f040ea05.png' alt='The web IDE served from the admin VM.'/>
<image src='ide-open-terminal.429243f9.png' alt='Opening a new terminal in the web IDE.'/>
nkp.deploy.intro:
Deploy something small by hand, so you can see what the console was doing for you.
A <white>Deployment</white> keeps your app running and replaces it when it dies.
<input/>
nkp.deploy.cmd: In your terminal, run: kubectl create deployment user{UserNum}-nkp-simple-app --image=nginx:1.27 Then watch it come up: kubectl get deployments
nkp.deploy.prompt: When user{UserNum}-nkp-simple-app shows as ready, type Ok to verify: <input var='Ok'/>
nkp.service.intro:
Your app runs, but nothing can reach it.
A <white>Service</white> gives it a stable address. Start with a <white>NodePort</white>, which opens the same port on every node.
<input/>
nkp.service.cmd: Expose the deployment: kubectl expose deployment/user{UserNum}-nkp-simple-app --type="NodePort" --port 80 Then find the port that was allocated: kubectl get service user{UserNum}-nkp-simple-app Browse to http://<any-node-ip>:<nodePort> for the NGINX welcome page.
nkp.service.prompt: When the NodePort answers, type Ok to verify: <input var='Ok'/>
nkp.lb.intro:
NodePort works, but it ties your app to node addresses, and nodes come and go.
A <white>LoadBalancer</white> service gets its own IP from <white>MetalLB</white>, which survives that.
<input/>
nkp.lb.cmd: Update the service in place rather than recreating it, so there is no downtime: kubectl patch service user{UserNum}-nkp-simple-app -p '{"spec":{"type":"LoadBalancer"}}' Watch for the address to appear: kubectl get service user{UserNum}-nkp-simple-app
nkp.lb.prompt: When EXTERNAL-IP is filled in and the page loads, type Ok to verify: <input var='Ok'/>
nkp.ingress.intro:
One external IP per app does not scale either.
An <white>Ingress</white> puts many apps behind one address, routed by hostname. <white>Traefik</white> does the routing here.
<input/>
nkp.ingress.yaml: Create simple-app-ingress.yaml in the IDE, then apply it with kubectl apply -f simple-app-ingress.yaml. Replace <ingress-lb-ip> with the management ingress IP (it ends in .16): apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1 kind: Ingress metadata: name: user{UserNum}-nkp-simple-app spec: ingressClassName: kommander-traefik rules: - host: user{UserNum}.<ingress-lb-ip>.sslip.io http: paths: - path: / pathType: Prefix backend: service: name: user{UserNum}-nkp-simple-app port: number: 80
nkp.ingress.prompt: When https://user{UserNum}.<ingress-lb-ip>.sslip.io serves NGINX, type Ok to verify: <input var='Ok'/>
